<title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

Currently, his lab focuses on the challenges of understanding the origin of life on Earth, and the construction of artificial cellular life in the laboratory.[8] They have conducted detailed studies of mechanisms by which RNA templates may have replicated on early earth before the emergence of enzyme catalysts. In particular, they have focused on imidazole-activated ribonucleotides (phosphorimidazolides) as monomers capable of elongating a new RNA strand.[9] Significantly, the Szostak group discovered that phosphorimidazolide-mediated template elongation occurs via 5'-5'-imidazolium bridged dinucleotide intermediates[10] which accelerate polymerization. Phosphorimidazolides were first proposed to be critical for early-earth nucleotide polymerization by Leslie E. Orgel and colleagues.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).

<document>
<title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).


</fragment>
<fragment>

Currently, his lab focuses on the challenges of understanding the origin of life on Earth, and the construction of artificial cellular life in the laboratory.[8] They have conducted detailed studies of mechanisms by which RNA templates may have replicated on early earth before the emergence of enzyme catalysts. In particular, they have focused on imidazole-activated ribonucleotides (phosphorimidazolides) as monomers capable of elongating a new RNA strand.[9] Significantly, the Szostak group discovered that phosphorimidazolide-mediated template elongation occurs via 5'-5'-imidazolium bridged dinucleotide intermediates[10] which accelerate polymerization. Phosphorimidazolides were first proposed to be critical for early-earth nucleotide polymerization by Leslie E. Orgel and colleagues.


</fragment>
<fragment>
6. **^** Szostak, Jack (February 1, 2009). "Ray Wu, as remembered by a former student". *Science in China Series C: Life Sciences*. **52** (2): 108–110. doi:10.1007/s11427-009-0023-6. PMID 19277516. S2CID 22028369.

<document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5] 


</fragment>
<fragment>
After her PhD, she held research fellowships in molecular biology at the Massachusetts General Hospital and in genetics at Harvard Medical School.[5] From 1991 to 1994, she was Lucille P. Markey Postdoctoral Scholar in Biomedical Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where she worked with Thomas Cech.[5] As of 2022[update], Doudna has an h-index of 141 according to Google Scholar[9] and of 111 according to Scopus.[29]

Doudna was an undergraduate student at Pomona College in Claremont, California, where she studied biochemistry.[10][11] During her freshman year, while taking a course in general chemistry, she questioned her own ability to pursue a career in science, and considered switching her major to French as a sophomore.[7][10] However, her French teacher suggested she stick with science.[10][7] Chemistry professors Fred Grieman and Corwin Hansch at Pomona had a major impact on her.[7] She started her first scientific research in the lab of professor Sharon Panasenko.[7] She earned her Bachelor of Arts degree in biochemistry in 1985.[7][27] She chose Harvard Medical School for her doctoral study and earned a PhD in Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology in 1989.[5][28] Her Ph.D. dissertation was on a system that increased the efficiency of a self-replicating catalytic RNA[14] and was supervised by Jack W. <document>
<title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

Currently, his lab focuses on the challenges of understanding the origin of life on Earth, and the construction of artificial cellular life in the laboratory.[8] They have conducted detailed studies of mechanisms by which RNA templates may have replicated on early earth before the emergence of enzyme catalysts. In particular, they have focused on imidazole-activated ribonucleotides (phosphorimidazolides) as monomers capable of elongating a new RNA strand.[9] Significantly, the Szostak group discovered that phosphorimidazolide-mediated template elongation occurs via 5'-5'-imidazolium bridged dinucleotide intermediates[10] which accelerate polymerization. Phosphorimidazolides were first proposed to be critical for early-earth nucleotide polymerization by Leslie E. Orgel and colleagues.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).


</fragment>

<document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5] 


</fragment>
<fragment>
After her PhD, she held research fellowships in molecular biology at the Massachusetts General Hospital and in genetics at Harvard Medical School.[5] From 1991 to 1994, she was Lucille P. Markey Postdoctoral Scholar in Biomedical Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where she worked with Thomas Cech.[5] As of 2022[update], Doudna has an h-index of 141 according to Google Scholar[9] and of 111 according to Scopus.[29]



### Research on ribozyme structure and function

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Doudna was an undergraduate student at Pomona College in Claremont, California, where she studied biochemistry.[10][11] During her freshman year, while taking a course in general chemistry, she questioned her own ability to pursue a career in science, and considered switching her major to French as a sophomore.[7][10] However, her French teacher suggested she stick with science.[10][7] Chemistry professors Fred Grieman and Corwin Hansch at Pomona had a major impact on her.[7] She started her first scientific research in the lab of professor Sharon Panasenko.[7] She earned her Bachelor of Arts degree in biochemistry in 1985.[7][27] She chose Harvard Medical School for her doctoral study and earned a PhD in Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology in 1989.[5][28] Her Ph.D. dissertation was on a system that increased the efficiency of a self-replicating catalytic RNA[14] and was supervised by Jack W. Szostak.[14]

<document>
<title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

Currently, his lab focuses on the challenges of understanding the origin of life on Earth, and the construction of artificial cellular life in the laboratory.[8] They have conducted detailed studies of mechanisms by which RNA templates may have replicated on early earth before the emergence of enzyme catalysts. In particular, they have focused on imidazole-activated ribonucleotides (phosphorimidazolides) as monomers capable of elongating a new RNA strand.[9] Significantly, the Szostak group discovered that phosphorimidazolide-mediated template elongation occurs via 5'-5'-imidazolium bridged dinucleotide intermediates[10] which accelerate polymerization. Phosphorimidazolides were first proposed to be critical for early-earth nucleotide polymerization by Leslie E. Orgel and colleagues.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).


</fragment>

<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>

Doudna was an undergraduate student at Pomona College in Claremont, California, where she studied biochemistry.[10][11] During her freshman year, while taking a course in general chemistry, she questioned her own ability to pursue a career in science, and considered switching her major to French as a sophomore.[7][10] However, her French teacher suggested she stick with science.[10][7] Chemistry professors Fred Grieman and Corwin Hansch at Pomona had a major impact on her.[7] She started her first scientific research in the lab of professor Sharon Panasenko.[7] She earned her Bachelor of Arts degree in biochemistry in 1985.[7][27] She chose Harvard Medical School for her doctoral study and earned a PhD in Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology in 1989.[5][28] Her Ph.D. dissertation was on a system that increased the efficiency of a self-replicating catalytic RNA[14] and was supervised by Jack W. Szostak.[14]

<fragment>

DAI covers doctoral dissertations accepted at accredited American institutions since 1861. Selected master's theses have been included since 1962; since 1988, the database includes citations for dissertations from 50 British universities that are available at The British Document Supply Centre.[5] Additionally, it covers a limited number of dissertations from the rest of the world.


The print version is published monthly and cumulated annually and it is available both in softcover and on microfiche. It is divided in three sections:



* Section A, Humanities and Social Sciences (ISSN 0419-4209)
* Section B, Sciences and Engineering (ISSN 0419-4217)
* Section C (formerly *European Dissertations*) (ISSN 1042-7279) covers non-North American materials, most of them unavailable for purchase from ProQuest. As of 2008, ProQuest no longer offers Section C as a separate product.


</fragment>
<fragment>

PQDT annually publishes more than 90% of all dissertations submitted from accredited institutions of higher learning in North America as well as from colleges and universities in Europe and Asia. Over the past 60 years, PQDT has amassed more than 1.4 million titles beginning with the first U.S. dissertation accepted by a university (Yale) in 1861. ProQuest began digitizing dissertations in 1997 from a microform archive.[3]


In October 2015, ProQuest added the ability for authors to include an ORCID identifier when submitting a thesis.[4]

<document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5] 


</fragment>
<fragment>
After her PhD, she held research fellowships in molecular biology at the Massachusetts General Hospital and in genetics at Harvard Medical School.[5] From 1991 to 1994, she was Lucille P. Markey Postdoctoral Scholar in Biomedical Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where she worked with Thomas Cech.[5] As of 2022[update], Doudna has an h-index of 141 according to Google Scholar[9] and of 111 according to Scopus.[29]

Doudna was an undergraduate student at Pomona College in Claremont, California, where she studied biochemistry.[10][11] During her freshman year, while taking a course in general chemistry, she questioned her own ability to pursue a career in science, and considered switching her major to French as a sophomore.[7][10] However, her French teacher suggested she stick with science.[10][7] Chemistry professors Fred Grieman and Corwin Hansch at Pomona had a major impact on her.[7] She started her first scientific research in the lab of professor Sharon Panasenko.[7] She earned her Bachelor of Arts degree in biochemistry in 1985.[7][27] She chose Harvard Medical School for her doctoral study and earned a PhD in Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology in 1989.[5][28] Her Ph.D. dissertation was on a system that increased the efficiency of a self-replicating catalytic RNA[14] and was supervised by Jack W. <title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5]

<title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).

<document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5] 


</fragment>
<fragment>
After her PhD, she held research fellowships in molecular biology at the Massachusetts General Hospital and in genetics at Harvard Medical School.[5] From 1991 to 1994, she was Lucille P. Markey Postdoctoral Scholar in Biomedical Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where she worked with Thomas Cech.[5] As of 2022[update], Doudna has an h-index of 141 according to Google Scholar[9] and of 111 according to Scopus.[29]



### Research on ribozyme structure and function

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Doudna was an undergraduate student at Pomona College in Claremont, California, where she studied biochemistry.[10][11] During her freshman year, while taking a course in general chemistry, she questioned her own ability to pursue a career in science, and considered switching her major to French as a sophomore.[7][10] However, her French teacher suggested she stick with science.[10][7] Chemistry professors Fred Grieman and Corwin Hansch at Pomona had a major impact on her.[7] She started her first scientific research in the lab of professor Sharon Panasenko.[7] She earned her Bachelor of Arts degree in biochemistry in 1985.[7][27] She chose Harvard Medical School for her doctoral study and earned a PhD in Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology in 1989.[5][28] Her Ph.D. dissertation was on a system that increased the efficiency of a self-replicating catalytic RNA[14] and was supervised by Jack W. Szostak.[14]

<document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5] 


</fragment>
<fragment>
After her PhD, she held research fellowships in molecular biology at the Massachusetts General Hospital and in genetics at Harvard Medical School.[5] From 1991 to 1994, she was Lucille P. Markey Postdoctoral Scholar in Biomedical Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where she worked with Thomas Cech.[5] As of 2022[update], Doudna has an h-index of 141 according to Google Scholar[9] and of 111 according to Scopus.[29]



### Research on ribozyme structure and function

[edit]

<document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5] 


</fragment>
<fragment>
After her PhD, she held research fellowships in molecular biology at the Massachusetts General Hospital and in genetics at Harvard Medical School.[5] From 1991 to 1994, she was Lucille P. Markey Postdoctoral Scholar in Biomedical Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where she worked with Thomas Cech.[5] As of 2022[update], Doudna has an h-index of 141 according to Google Scholar[9] and of 111 according to Scopus.[29]



### Research on ribozyme structure and function

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Doudna was an undergraduate student at Pomona College in Claremont, California, where she studied biochemistry.[10][11] During her freshman year, while taking a course in general chemistry, she questioned her own ability to pursue a career in science, and considered switching her major to French as a sophomore.[7][10] However, her French teacher suggested she stick with science.[10][7] Chemistry professors Fred Grieman and Corwin Hansch at Pomona had a major impact on her.[7] She started her first scientific research in the lab of professor Sharon Panasenko.[7] She earned her Bachelor of Arts degree in biochemistry in 1985.[7][27] She chose Harvard Medical School for her doctoral study and earned a PhD in Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology in 1989.[5][28] Her Ph.D. dissertation was on a system that increased the efficiency of a self-replicating catalytic RNA[14] and was supervised by Jack W. Szostak.[14]



## Career and research

<document>
<title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).


</fragment>

Currently, his lab focuses on the challenges of understanding the origin of life on Earth, and the construction of artificial cellular life in the laboratory.[8] They have conducted detailed studies of mechanisms by which RNA templates may have replicated on early earth before the emergence of enzyme catalysts. In particular, they have focused on imidazole-activated ribonucleotides (phosphorimidazolides) as monomers capable of elongating a new RNA strand.[9] Significantly, the Szostak group discovered that phosphorimidazolide-mediated template elongation occurs via 5'-5'-imidazolium bridged dinucleotide intermediates[10] which accelerate polymerization. <document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5] 


</fragment>

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).


</fragment>
<fragment>

Currently, his lab focuses on the challenges of understanding the origin of life on Earth, and the construction of artificial cellular life in the laboratory.[8] They have conducted detailed studies of mechanisms by which RNA templates may have replicated on early earth before the emergence of enzyme catalysts. In particular, they have focused on imidazole-activated ribonucleotides (phosphorimidazolides) as monomers capable of elongating a new RNA strand.[9] Significantly, the Szostak group discovered that phosphorimidazolide-mediated template elongation occurs via 5'-5'-imidazolium bridged dinucleotide intermediates[10] which accelerate polymerization. Phosphorimidazolides were first proposed to be critical for early-earth nucleotide polymerization by Leslie E. Orgel and colleagues.


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Self-replication</title>
<fragment>
* Biology: studies of organismal and cellular natural replication and replicators, and their interaction, including sub-disciplines such as population dynamics, quorum sensing, autophagy pathways. These can be an important guide to avoid design difficulties in self-replicating machinery.
* Chemistry: self-replication studies are typically about how a specific set of molecules can act together to replicate each other within the set[14] (often part of Systems chemistry field).
* Biochemistry: simple systems of *in vitro* ribosomal self replication have been attempted,[15] but as of January 2021, indefinite *in vitro* ribosomal self replication has not been achieved in the lab.
* Nanotechnology or more precisely, molecular nanotechnology is concerned with making nano scale assemblers. Without self-replication, capital and assembly costs of molecular machines become impossibly large. Many bottom-up approaches to nanotechnology take advantage of biochemical or chemical self-assembly.

</fragment>
</document>

<title>Ligase ribozyme</title>
<fragment>

In order to copy RNA, fragments or monomers (individual building blocks) that have 5′-triphosphates must be ligated together. This is true for modern (protein-based) polymerases, and is also the most likely mechanism by which a ribozyme self-replicase in an RNA world might function. Yet no one has found a natural ribozyme that can perform this reaction.

<title>Thomas Cech</title>
<fragment>
Cech's main research area is that of the process of transcription in the nucleus of cells. He studies how the genetic code of DNA is transcribed into RNA. In the 1970s, Cech had been studying the splicing of RNA in the unicellular organism *Tetrahymena thermophila* when he discovered that an unprocessed RNA molecule could splice itself. In 1982, Cech became the first to show that RNA molecules are not restricted to being passive carriers of genetic information – they can have catalytic functions and can participate in cellular reactions.[7] RNA-processing reactions and protein synthesis on ribosomes in particular are catalysed by RNA. RNA enzymes are known as ribozymes and have provided a new tool for gene technology. They also have the potential to provide new therapeutic agents – for example, they have the ability to destroy and cleave invading, viral RNAs.

This should be able to happen in prebiotically plausible conditions with high rates of copying accuracy to prevent degradation of information but also allowing for the occurrence of occasional errors during the copying process to allow for Darwinian evolution to proceed.[4]


Attempts have been made to develop ribozymes as therapeutic agents, as enzymes which target defined RNA sequences for cleavage, as biosensors, and for applications in functional genomics and gene discovery.[5]

<title>Leslie Orgel</title>
<fragment>
[edit]

In the late 1960s, Orgel proposed that life was based on RNA before it was based on DNA or proteins. His theory included genes based on RNA and RNA enzymes.[17] This view would be developed and shaped into the now widely accepted RNA world hypothesis.


Almost thirty years later, Orgel wrote a lengthy review of the RNA World hypothesis.[18] This review highlighted many proposed syntheses for RNA and its parts in abiotic conditions, noted the significance of the discovery of ribozymes (RNA molecules that function as enzymes just as Orgel had once predicted) and at the same time, demonstrated nucleic acid polymers with alternatives to ribose such as threose nucleic acid (TNA) and peptide nucleic acid (PNA).


In conclusion, Orgel wrote, "One must recognize that, despite considerable progress, the problem of the origin of the RNA World is far from being solved."[18]



## Awards

[edit]


</fragment>

Montmorillonite clay was also shown to promote the polymerization of adenosine phosphorimidazolide into oligonucleotides tens of bases in length starting from a poly-adenosine 10-mer primer.[15] In the absence of montmorillonite, the primer was capped through the formation of a 5’ adenosine pyrophosphate.


The oligonucleotide products in early studies were typically characterized through a combination of 14C radiolabeling, gel electrophoresis, and paper electrophoresis. Though he later downplayed the hypothesis, Orgel, along with Francis Crick, proposed a detailed panspermia scenario for the origin of life on Earth, going so far as to suggest that life on Earth was designed by an alien species and sent to Earth.[16] They proposed a design for the spaceship that aliens could have used to seed life on Earth.

## Towards Self-Replicating RNA Systems (英语)

Based on my research using Wikipedia, I'd like to explore the fascinating and challenging frontier of RNA self-replication. This quest stands at the intersection of molecular biology, biochemistry, and origins-of-life research, representing one of biology's most fundamental puzzles.

### Historical Context: The RNA World Hypothesis

The concept of RNA-based life largely originates from the **RNA world hypothesis**, first systematically proposed by **Leslie Orgel** in the late 1960s. Orgel envisioned early life based on RNA genes and RNA enzymes before the emergence of DNA and proteins. This theoretical framework gained substantial empirical support with the groundbreaking discovery by **Thomas Cech** in 1982, who demonstrated that unprocessed RNA molecules could splice themselves—revealing RNA molecules are not merely passive genetic carriers but can have catalytic functions.

Cech's work with *Tetrahymena thermophila* showed that RNA processing reactions can be catalyzed by RNA itself. These RNA enzymes, termed **ribozymes**, provided the missing mechanistic link supporting Orgel's decades-old prediction. As the ribozyme Wikipedia article notes, researchers investigating life's origins have been searching for ribozymes capable of self-replication—requiring catalytic synthesis of RNA polymers with sufficient accuracy to preserve information while allowing evolutionary variation.

### In Vitro Evolution: Engineering New Ribozymes

The systematic discovery of ribozymes with novel catalytic capabilities began with the development of **in vitro evolution** techniques. **David Bartel**, working in **Jack Szostak's** laboratory, pioneered the isolation of the first ribozymes directly from random sequence pools using systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX).

Bartel's notable achievements include:
- Isolation of the **Class I ligase ribozyme** from random sequences
- Evolution of this ligase to function as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase capable of extending primers on external RNA templates
- Providing crucial experimental support for the RNA world theory

The approach typically involves:
1. Starting with vast libraries of random RNA sequences (10^15 variants)
2. Iterative selection cycles for desired catalytic activities
3. Amplification of successful sequences
4. Optimization through mutagenesis and re-selection

### Catalytic Mechanisms: Metal Ion-Dependent Chemistry

Research by **Scott Strobel** and others has revealed the sophisticated catalytic mechanisms employed by ribozymes. Strobel's group developed nucleotide analog interference mapping to identify critical functional groups in structured RNAs and solved crystal structures of various catalytic RNAs.

Key mechanistic insights include:
- Metal ion cofactors (often Mg²⁺) play crucial catalytic roles
- Ribozymes can achieve sophisticated tertiary folding to create active sites
- The **Azoarcus Group I catalytic intron** structure revealed how RNA can achieve precise molecular recognition and chemistry

### Major Technical Obstacles

#### 1. Template-Directed Polymerization Challenge

The **ligase ribozyme** article highlights that copying RNA requires fragments or monomers with 5′-triphosphates to be ligated together—the same mechanism used by modern protein polymerases. However, naturally occurring ribozymes that perform this reaction have not been found, necessitating extensive engineering efforts.

#### 2. Length and Specificity Limitations

While ligase ribozymes can join two RNA segments, extending them to polymerize dozens of nucleotides with sequence-specific fidelity has proven exceptionally difficult. The catalytic efficiency drops dramatically as required polymerization length increases.

#### 3. Prebiotic Plausibility Questions

Even if technically achievable, creating RNA replication systems under prebiotically plausible conditions remains challenging. This involves:
- Availability of activated nucleotides in early Earth environments
- Overcoming competing hydrolysis reactions
- Maintaining suitable ionic and temperature conditions

### Notable Experimental Advances

#### The Joyce-Lincoln Self-Sustaining RNA System

Perhaps the most significant advance toward self-replication came from **Gerald Joyce** and **Tracey Lincoln** in 2009. Their work demonstrated **self-sustained replication of an RNA enzyme**—a system where two ribozymes catalyze each other's synthesis in a cross-catalytic cycle.

Key features of this breakthrough:
- Engineered ribozymes that function as both template and catalyst
- Demonstrated exponential amplification capabilities
- Provided experimental validation of **autocatalytic set** concepts developed by **Stuart Kauffman**

This system represents the closest laboratory approach to achieving true RNA self-replication, though it still differs from linear template-directed polymerization.

#### Structural and Biochemical Insights

Research by multiple groups has revealed:
- **Hammerhead ribozymes** and other small catalytic RNAs demonstrate fundamental RNA chemical capabilities
- **Ribosomal RNA** shows modern biology's retention of RNA catalytic functions
- Crystallographic studies (including those solving structures like the glmS ribozyme) provide templates for rational design

### Theoretical Frameworks

#### Hypercycle and Autocatalytic Set Theories

**Manfred Eigen** developed hypercycle theory as a mathematical framework for understanding how self-replicating systems could organize and evolve. While initially applied to hypothetical replicators, these concepts now find experimental validation in ribozyme research.

#### Alternative Nucleic Acid Systems

Orgel's later work highlighted the search for **alternative nucleic acid polymers** (如threose nucleic acid, peptide nucleic acid) that might have preceded or coexisted with RNA in early evolution. The fundamental catalytic principles discovered for RNA ribozymes might extend to these alternative systems.

### Current Frontiers and Future Directions

The field continues to progress along several complementary approaches:

#### Engineering Better Polymerases

Efforts to evolve ribozyme polymerases focus on:
- Increasing catalytic turnover rates
- Expanding substrate specificity
- Improving fidelity and error-correction mechanisms
- Achieving longer template-directed synthesis

#### Prebiotic Chemistry Integration

Researchers are working to bridge the gap between laboratory engineering and plausible early Earth conditions, including:
- Mineral surface catalysis (notably montmorillonite clay)
- Non-enzymatic template-directed polymerization
- Energy input mechanisms (thermal gradients, wet-dry cycles)

#### Synthetic Approaches

Some laboratories, like **Phil Holliger's** group, have explored **synthetic genetic polymers** (XNAs) capable of heredity and evolution, potentially circumventing some of RNA's chemical constraints while maintaining its replication principles.

### Fundamental Implications

Success in creating robust RNA self-replication systems would have profound implications for:

1. **Origins of Life research**: Providing experimental validation for RNA world scenarios
2. **Synthetic biology**: Creating novel self-replicating systems for biotechnology
3. **Evolutionary biology**: Understanding fundamental principles of molecular evolution
4. **Astrobiology**: Informing the search for life based on alternative biochemistries

### Conclusion: The Ongoing Quest

While true linear template-directed RNA self-replication remains elusive, cumulative progress over several decades has brought researchers closer to this goal. The Joyce-Lincoln cross-catalytic system represents a major milestone, demonstrating principal feasibility while highlighting remaining challenges.

As research continues, advances in directed evolution techniques, structural biology, and prebiotic chemistry converge on this fundamental question. The pursuit of an RNA self-replicase not only addresses life's historical origins but also expands our understanding of molecular catalysis and the boundaries between chemistry and biology.

The quest exemplifies how historical scientific debates—dating back to Orgel's theoretical proposals—can stimulate decades of experimental research, ultimately producing both fundamental insights and practical methodologies that may one day achieve what once seemed impossible: creating life's molecular ancestor in the laboratory.

---

*I have drawn mainly on Wikipedia articles about Key figures (Thomas Cech, David Bartel, Gerald Joyce, Jack Szostak, Leslie Orgel, Manfred Eigen, Scott Strobel), Key concepts (RNA world hypothesis, ribozymes, ligase ribozymes, autocatalytic sets, SELEX), and Key discoveries (self-sustained replication of RNA enzymes) to construct this overview of RNA self-replication research.*

The field continues to progress along several complementary approaches:

#### Engineering Better Polymerases

Efforts to evolve ribozyme polymerases focus on:
- Increasing catalytic turnover rates
- Expanding substrate specificity
- Improving fidelity and error-correction mechanisms
- Achieving longer template-directed synthesis

#### Prebiotic Chemistry Integration

Researchers are working to bridge the gap between laboratory engineering and plausible early Earth conditions, including:
- Mineral surface catalysis (notably montmorillonite clay)
- Non-enzymatic template-directed polymerization
- Energy input mechanisms (thermal gradients, wet-dry cycles)

#### Synthetic Approaches

Some laboratories, like **Phil Holliger's** group, have explored **synthetic genetic polymers** (XNAs) capable of heredity and evolution, potentially circumventing some of RNA's chemical constraints while maintaining its replication principles.

### Fundamental Implications

Success in creating robust RNA self-replication systems would have profound implications for:

1. **Origins of Life research**: Providing experimental validation for RNA world scenarios
2. **Synthetic biology**: Creating novel self-replicating systems for biotechnology
3. **Evolutionary biology**: Understanding fundamental principles of molecular evolution
4. **Astrobiology**: Informing the search for life based on alternative biochemistries

### Conclusion: The Ongoing Quest

While true linear template-directed RNA self-replication remains elusive, cumulative progress over several decades has brought researchers closer to this goal. The Joyce-Lincoln cross-catalytic system represents a major milestone, demonstrating principal feasibility while highlighting remaining challenges.

As research continues, advances in directed evolution techniques, structural biology, and prebiotic chemistry converge on this fundamental question. The pursuit of an RNA self-replicase not only addresses life's historical origins but also expands our understanding of molecular catalysis and the boundaries between chemistry and biology.

The quest exemplifies how historical scientific debates—dating back to Orgel's theoretical proposals—can stimulate decades of experimental research, ultimately producing both fundamental insights and practical methodologies that may one day achieve what once seemed impossible: creating life's molecular ancestor in the laboratory.

## Towards Self-Replicating RNA Systems (英语)

Based on my research using Wikipedia, I'd like to explore the fascinating and challenging frontier of RNA self-replication. This quest stands at the intersection of molecular biology, biochemistry, and origins-of-life research, representing one of biology's most fundamental puzzles.

### Historical Context: The RNA World Hypothesis

The concept of RNA-based life largely originates from the **RNA world hypothesis**, first systematically proposed by **Leslie Orgel** in the late 1960s. Orgel envisioned early life based on RNA genes and RNA enzymes before the emergence of DNA and proteins. This theoretical framework gained substantial empirical support with the groundbreaking discovery by **Thomas Cech** in 1982, who demonstrated that unprocessed RNA molecules could splice themselves—revealing RNA molecules are not merely passive genetic carriers but can have catalytic functions.

Cech's work with *Tetrahymena thermophila* showed that RNA processing reactions can be catalyzed by RNA itself. These RNA enzymes, termed **ribozymes**, provided the missing mechanistic link supporting Orgel's decades-old prediction. As the ribozyme Wikipedia article notes, researchers investigating life's origins have been searching for ribozymes capable of self-replication—requiring catalytic synthesis of RNA polymers with sufficient accuracy to preserve information while allowing evolutionary variation.

### In Vitro Evolution: Engineering New Ribozymes

The systematic discovery of ribozymes with novel catalytic capabilities began with the development of **in vitro evolution** techniques. **David Bartel**, working in **Jack Szostak's** laboratory, pioneered the isolation of the first ribozymes directly from random sequence pools using systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX).

Bartel's notable achievements include:
- Isolation of the **Class I ligase ribozyme** from random sequences
- Evolution of this ligase to function as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase capable of extending primers on external RNA templates
- Providing crucial experimental support for the RNA world theory

The approach typically involves:
1. Starting with vast libraries of random RNA sequences (10^15 variants)
2. Iterative selection cycles for desired catalytic activities
3. Amplification of successful sequences
4. Optimization through mutagenesis and re-selection

### Catalytic Mechanisms: Metal Ion-Dependent Chemistry

Research by **Scott Strobel** and others has revealed the sophisticated catalytic mechanisms employed by ribozymes. Strobel's group developed nucleotide analog interference mapping to identify critical functional groups in structured RNAs and solved crystal structures of various catalytic RNAs.

Key mechanistic insights include:
- Metal ion cofactors (often Mg²⁺) play crucial catalytic roles
- Ribozymes can achieve sophisticated tertiary folding to create active sites
- The **Azoarcus Group I catalytic intron** structure revealed how RNA can achieve precise molecular recognition and chemistry

### Major Technical Obstacles

#### 1. Template-Directed Polymerization Challenge

The **ligase ribozyme** article highlights that copying RNA requires fragments or monomers with 5′-triphosphates to be ligated together—the same mechanism used by modern protein polymerases. However, naturally occurring ribozymes that perform this reaction have not been found, necessitating extensive engineering efforts.

#### 2. Length and Specificity Limitations

While ligase ribozymes can join two RNA segments, extending them to polymerize dozens of nucleotides with sequence-specific fidelity has proven exceptionally difficult. The catalytic efficiency drops dramatically as required polymerization length increases.

#### 3. Prebiotic Plausibility Questions

Even if technically achievable, creating RNA replication systems under prebiotically plausible conditions remains challenging. This involves:
- Availability of activated nucleotides in early Earth environments
- Overcoming competing hydrolysis reactions
- Maintaining suitable ionic and temperature conditions

### Notable Experimental Advances

#### The Joyce-Lincoln Self-Sustaining RNA System

Perhaps the most significant advance toward self-replication came from **Gerald Joyce** and **Tracey Lincoln** in 2009. Their work demonstrated **self-sustained replication of an RNA enzyme**—a system where two ribozymes catalyze each other's synthesis in a cross-catalytic cycle.

Key features of this breakthrough:
- Engineered ribozymes that function as both template and catalyst
- Demonstrated exponential amplification capabilities
- Provided experimental validation of **autocatalytic set** concepts developed by **Stuart Kauffman**

This system represents the closest laboratory approach to achieving true RNA self-replication, though it still differs from linear template-directed polymerization.

#### Structural and Biochemical Insights

Research by multiple groups has revealed:
- **Hammerhead ribozymes** and other small catalytic RNAs demonstrate fundamental RNA chemical capabilities
- **Ribosomal RNA** shows modern biology's retention of RNA catalytic functions
- Crystallographic studies (including those solving structures like the glmS ribozyme) provide templates for rational design

### Theoretical Frameworks

#### Hypercycle and Autocatalytic Set Theories

**Manfred Eigen** developed hypercycle theory as a mathematical framework for understanding how self-replicating systems could organize and evolve. While initially applied to hypothetical replicators, these concepts now find experimental validation in ribozyme research.

#### Alternative Nucleic Acid Systems

Orgel's later work highlighted the search for **alternative nucleic acid polymers** (如threose nucleic acid, peptide nucleic acid) that might have preceded or coexisted with RNA in early evolution. The fundamental catalytic principles discovered for RNA ribozymes might extend to these alternative systems.

### Current Frontiers and Future Directions

The field continues to progress along several complementary approaches:

#### Engineering Better Polymerases

Efforts to evolve ribozyme polymerases focus on:
- Increasing catalytic turnover rates
- Expanding substrate specificity
- Improving fidelity and error-correction mechanisms

2. **Synthetic biology**: Creating novel self-replicating systems for biotechnology
3. **Evolutionary biology**: Understanding fundamental principles of molecular evolution
4. **Astrobiology**: Informing the search for life based on alternative biochemistries

As research continues, advances in directed evolution techniques, structural biology, and prebiotic chemistry converge on this fundamental question. <title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).

<document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5] 


</fragment>
<fragment>
After her PhD, she held research fellowships in molecular biology at the Massachusetts General Hospital and in genetics at Harvard Medical School.[5] From 1991 to 1994, she was Lucille P. Markey Postdoctoral Scholar in Biomedical Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where she worked with Thomas Cech.[5] As of 2022[update], Doudna has an h-index of 141 according to Google Scholar[9] and of 111 according to Scopus.[29]



### Research on ribozyme structure and function

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Doudna was an undergraduate student at Pomona College in Claremont, California, where she studied biochemistry.[10][11] During her freshman year, while taking a course in general chemistry, she questioned her own ability to pursue a career in science, and considered switching her major to French as a sophomore.[7][10] However, her French teacher suggested she stick with science.[10][7] Chemistry professors Fred Grieman and Corwin Hansch at Pomona had a major impact on her.[7] She started her first scientific research in the lab of professor Sharon Panasenko.[7] She earned her Bachelor of Arts degree in biochemistry in 1985.[7][27] She chose Harvard Medical School for her doctoral study and earned a PhD in Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology in 1989.[5][28] Her Ph.D. dissertation was on a system that increased the efficiency of a self-replicating catalytic RNA[14] and was supervised by Jack W. Szostak.[14]

<document>
<title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).


</fragment>
<fragment>

Currently, his lab focuses on the challenges of understanding the origin of life on Earth, and the construction of artificial cellular life in the laboratory.[8] They have conducted detailed studies of mechanisms by which RNA templates may have replicated on early earth before the emergence of enzyme catalysts. In particular, they have focused on imidazole-activated ribonucleotides (phosphorimidazolides) as monomers capable of elongating a new RNA strand.[9] Significantly, the Szostak group discovered that phosphorimidazolide-mediated template elongation occurs via 5'-5'-imidazolium bridged dinucleotide intermediates[10] which accelerate polymerization. Phosphorimidazolides were first proposed to be critical for early-earth nucleotide polymerization by Leslie E. Orgel and colleagues.


</fragment>
<fragment>
6. **^** Szostak, Jack (February 1, 2009). "Ray Wu, as remembered by a former student". *Science in China Series C: Life Sciences*. **52** (2): 108–110. doi:10.1007/s11427-009-0023-6. PMID 19277516. S2CID 22028369.

<document>
<title>Ribozyme</title>
<fragment>

Researchers who are investigating the origins of life through the RNA world hypothesis have been working on discovering a ribozyme with the capacity to self-replicate, which would require it to have the ability to catalytically synthesize polymers of RNA. This should be able to happen in prebiotically plausible conditions with high rates of copying accuracy to prevent degradation of information but also allowing for the occurrence of occasional errors during the copying process to allow for Darwinian evolution to proceed.[4]


Attempts have been made to develop ribozymes as therapeutic agents, as enzymes which target defined RNA sequences for cleavage, as biosensors, and for applications in functional genomics and gene discovery.[5]




## Discovery

<document>
<title>Ligase ribozyme</title>
<fragment>

In order to copy RNA, fragments or monomers (individual building blocks) that have 5′-triphosphates must be ligated together. This is true for modern (protein-based) polymerases, and is also the most likely mechanism by which a ribozyme self-replicase in an RNA world might function. Yet no one has found a natural ribozyme that can perform this reaction.




## In vitro evolution and selection

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** Robertson MP, Hesselberth JR, Ellington AD (April 2001). "Optimization and optimality of a short ribozyme ligase that joins non-Watson-Crick base pairings". *RNA*. **7** (4): 513–523. doi:10.1017/S1355838201002199. PMC 1370105. PMID 11345430.
2. **^** Robertson MP, Scott WG (March 2007). "The structural basis of ribozyme-catalyzed RNA assembly". *Science*. **315** (5818): 1549–1553. doi:10.1126/science.1136231. PMID 17363667. S2CID 11530091.
3. **^** Joyce GF (March 2007). "Structural biology. A glimpse of biology's first enzyme". *Science*. **315** (5818): 1507–1508. doi:10.1126/science.1140736. PMID 17363651. S2CID 82057900.

## Further reading

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Crystal structure of the Class I ligase ribozyme at 2.98 Å resolution (PDB ID: 3HHN). The phosphodiester bond formed by this enzyme is shown as spheres.
![](image)The L1 Ligase Ribozyme 2.6 Å crystal structure
The RNA **Ligase ribozyme** was the first of several types of synthetic ribozymes produced by in vitro evolution and selection techniques. They are an important class of ribozymes because they catalyze the assembly of RNA fragments into phosphodiester RNA polymers, a reaction required of all extant nucleic acid polymerases and thought to be required for any self-replicating molecule. Ideas that the origin of life may have involved the first self-replicating molecules being ribozymes are called RNA World hypotheses. Ligase ribozymes may have been part of such a pre-biotic RNA world.


</fragment>
<fragment>
RNA in vitro evolution or SELEX enables the artificial evolution and selection of RNA molecules that possess a desired property, such as binding affinity for a particular ligand or an activity such as that of an enzyme or catalyst. The first such selections involved isolation of various aptamers that bind to small molecules. The first catalytic RNAs produced by in vitro evolution were RNA ligases, catalytic RNAs that join two RNA fragments to produce a single adduct. The most active ligase known to date is the Class I ligase, isolated from random sequence (work of David Bartel, while in the Szostak lab). Other examples of RNA ligases include the L1 ligase (Robertson and Ellington), the R3C ligase (Joyce), the DSL ligase (Inoue). All these ligases catalyze the formation of a 3′–5′ phosphodiester bond between two RNA fragments.



## The L1 ligase

[edit]


</fragment>

<fragment>
Each RNA polymerase ribozyme was engineered to remain linked to its new, synthesized RNA strand; this allowed the team to isolate successful polymerases. The isolated RNA polymerases were again used for another round of evolution. After several rounds of evolution, they obtained one RNA polymerase ribozyme called 24-3 that was able to copy almost any other RNA, from small catalysts to long RNA-based enzymes. Particular RNAs were amplified up to 10,000 times, a first RNA version of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR).[30]
Catalysis

</fragment>
<fragment>

These chains have been proposed by some as the first, primitive forms of life. In an RNA world, different sets of RNA strands would have had different replication outputs, which would have increased or decreased their frequency in the population, i.e., natural selection. As the fittest sets of RNA molecules expanded their numbers, novel catalytic properties added by mutation, which benefitted their persistence and expansion, could accumulate in the population. Such an autocatalytic set of ribozymes, capable of self-replication in about an hour, has been identified. It was produced by molecular competition (*in vitro* evolution) of candidate enzyme mixtures.[70]

![](image)Stylized rendering of the full-length  
 hammerhead ribozyme RNA molecule
The **hammerhead ribozyme** is an RNA motif that catalyzes reversible cleavage and ligation reactions at a specific site within an RNA molecule. It is one of several catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) known to occur in nature. It serves as a model system for research on the structure and properties of RNA, and is used for targeted RNA cleavage experiments, some with proposed therapeutic applications. Named for the resemblance of early secondary structure diagrams to a hammerhead shark,[1] hammerhead ribozymes were originally discovered in two classes of plant virus-like RNAs: satellite RNAs and viroids. They are also known in some classes of retrotransposons, including the retrozymes.[2] The hammerhead ribozyme motif has been ubiquitously reported in lineages across the tree of life.[3][4]

Based on the Wikipedia sources I consulted, I can provide a comprehensive explanation of the chemistry of nucleotide condensation and polymerization by ribozymes:

## The Chemistry of Nucleotide Condensation in Ribozymes

### **Fundamental Chemical Reaction**

Nucleotide condensation by ribozymes forms **phosphodiester bonds** through a classic phosphoryl transfer reaction. This involves the nucleophilic attack of the 3'-hydroxyl group of one nucleotide on the α-phosphate of another nucleotide, resulting in the formation of a phosphodiester bond and the release of pyrophosphate (PPi) when using NTPs.

### **Key Chemical Components from the Wikipedia Sources**

From the ligase ribozyme entry, the chemistry involves **5′-triphosphate nucleotides** that must be joined together - the same chemistry used by modern protein polymerases. The reaction forms a **3′–5′ phosphodiester bond** between RNA fragments.

### **Catalytic Mechanism**

While the detailed catalytic chemistry wasn't fully covered in the sources I found, based on general ribozyme chemistry:

1. **Metal Ion Catalysis**: Most ribozymes, including polymerase ribozymes, use **divalent metal ions (particularly Mg²⁺)** to:
   - Stabilize the negative charges on the phosphate backbone
   - Activate the nucleophilic 3'-OH group
   - Position substrates correctly for reaction

2. **General Acid-Base Chemistry**: The ribozyme provides both:
   - **General base** activation of the 3'-OH nucleophile
   - **General acid** stabilization of the leaving group

### **Types of Ribozymal Condensation Reactions**

From the sources, ribozymes can catalyze:

1. **RNA Ligation** (Ligase ribozymes):
   - Join pre-existing RNA fragments
   - Class I ligase, L1 ligase, R3C ligase, DSL ligase
   - Catalyze formation of phosphodiester bonds between RNA fragments

2. **RNA Polymerization** (Evolved polymerase ribozymes):
   - Build RNA chains from nucleotide monomers
   - One evolved ribozyme called "24-3" could amplify RNAs up to 10,000-fold
   - Represents an RNA version of PCR

3. **Self-Cleavage/Ligation** (Hammerhead ribozymes):
   - Catalyze both cleavage and ligation at specific sites
   - Reversible chemistry that can both form and break phosphodiester bonds

### **Chemical Evolutionary Significance**

According to the RNA world entry, these ribozymal reactions are crucial for:
- **Self-replication**: Required for any self-replicating molecule
- **Natural selection**: Different replication outputs create evolutionary pressure
- **Complexity development**: Novel catalytic properties can accumulate through mutation

### **Key Chemical Features**

From the group II intron and hammerhead ribozyme sources, the chemistry involves:
- **Tertiary structure organization** to create an active site
- **Catalytic core formation** that positions reactants
- **Energy coupling** through the high-energy phosphate bonds of NTPs
- **Stereochemistry control** to ensure proper bond formation

### **Limitations and Evolution**

The sources note that no **natural ribozyme** has been found that can efficiently perform general RNA polymerization reactions - most efficient polymerase ribozymes have been created through **in vitro evolution** in laboratory settings. The Class I ligase, mentioned in the sources, was isolated from random sequence pools through directed evolution.

This chemistry represents the foundation of how life could have transitioned from an RNA-only world to the current protein-dominated biochemistry, with ribozymes providing the template for modern enzyme catalysis while using the same fundamental chemical principles.

<document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5] 


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Shape of a self-splicing intron with two exons (shown in red and blue). DS Goodsell, 2005, PDB
At Yale, Doudna's group was able to crystallize and solve the three-dimensional structure of the catalytic core of the *Tetrahymena* Group I ribozyme.[7] They showed that a core of five magnesium ions clustered in one region of the P4-P6 domain of the ribozyme, forming a hydrophobic core around which the rest of the structure could fold.[7] This is analogous, but chemically distinct from, the way proteins typically have a core of hydrophobic amino acids.[7] Her group has crystallized other ribozymes,[14] including the Hepatitis Delta Virus ribozyme.[7] This initial work to solve large RNA structures led to further structural studies on an internal ribosome entry site(IRES) and protein-RNA complexes such as the Signal Recognition Particle.[7]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Doudna was introduced to CRISPR by Jillian Banfield in 2006 who had found Doudna by way of a Google search, having typed "RNAi and UC Berkeley" into her browser, and Doudna's name came up at the top of the list.[32][33] In 2012, Doudna and her colleagues made a new discovery that reduces the time and work needed to edit genomic DNA.[34][35] Their discovery relies on a protein named Cas9 found in the *Streptococcus* bacterial "CRISPR" immune system that cooperates with guide RNA and works like scissors. The protein attacks its prey, the DNA of viruses, and slices it up, preventing it from infecting the bacterium.[11] This system was first discovered by Yoshizumi Ishino and colleagues in 1987[36] and later characterized by Francisco Mojica,[37] but Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed for the first time that they could use different RNAs to program it to cut and edit different DNAs.[11]


</fragment>

<document>
<title>Ribozyme</title>
<fragment>
In the 1980s, Thomas Cech, at the University of Colorado Boulder, was studying the excision of introns in a ribosomal RNA gene in *Tetrahymena thermophila*. While trying to purify the enzyme responsible for the splicing reaction, he found that the intron could be spliced out in the absence of any added cell extract. As much as they tried, Cech and his colleagues could not identify any protein associated with the splicing reaction. After much work, Cech proposed that the intron sequence portion of the RNA could break and reform phosphodiester bonds. At about the same time, Sidney Altman, a professor at Yale University, was studying the way tRNA molecules are processed in the cell when he and his colleagues isolated an enzyme called RNase-P, which is responsible for conversion of a precursor tRNA into the active tRNA. Much to their surprise, they found that RNase-P contained RNA in addition to protein and that RNA was an essential component of the active enzyme. 
</fragment>

<document>
<title>Jack W. Szostak</title>
<fragment>

Currently, his lab focuses on the challenges of understanding the origin of life on Earth, and the construction of artificial cellular life in the laboratory.[8] They have conducted detailed studies of mechanisms by which RNA templates may have replicated on early earth before the emergence of enzyme catalysts. In particular, they have focused on imidazole-activated ribonucleotides (phosphorimidazolides) as monomers capable of elongating a new RNA strand.[9] Significantly, the Szostak group discovered that phosphorimidazolide-mediated template elongation occurs via 5'-5'-imidazolium bridged dinucleotide intermediates[10] which accelerate polymerization. Phosphorimidazolides were first proposed to be critical for early-earth nucleotide polymerization by Leslie E. Orgel and colleagues.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In the early 90s his laboratory shifted its research direction and focused on studying RNA enzymes, which had been recently discovered by Cech and Altman. He developed the technique of in vitro evolution of RNA (also developed independently by Gerald Joyce) which enables the discovery of RNAs with desired functions through successive cycles of selection, amplification and mutation. He isolated the first aptamer (term he used for the first time). He isolated RNA enzymes with RNA ligase activity directly from random sequence (project of David Bartel).


</fragment>

<title>Tetrahymena thermophila</title>
<fragment>

In 1953, the MAT locus in this species was first described by David L. Nanney.[12]


In 1982, the group 1 intron was discovered located in the rRNA transcript of this species[21]: 82 by Thomas Cech and his coworks.[22]: 205 This was considered the first ribozyme that can self-splice from a primary transcript without the help of proteins.[21]: 82 Cech also later on discovered enzymatic RNA in this species.[23]


Telomerase and telomeres were first discovered in this species as well[24] by Elizabeth Blackburn and Carol Greider.[25][26]


The first report of HAT activity was reported in this species in the year 1995.[27] As well as the first type A HAT was discovered in this species.[28]

Based on my research of the relevant literature, here's a detailed explanation of how ribozyme research in the 1980s and 1990s addressed the issue of needing rare combinations of amino acids to form functional proteins, as part of the broader effort to support the RNA world hypothesis:

## The Central Challenge to the RNA World Hypothesis

The RNA world hypothesis proposes that early life used RNA both for genetic information storage and catalytic functions, before proteins and DNA evolved. However, this faced a significant chicken-and-egg problem: while ribozymes (RNA enzymes) could theoretically provide the catalytic functions needed for early life, they seemed much less efficient and versatile than protein enzymes. The key question was: **Could RNA molecules alone have provided sufficient catalytic capabilities to bootstrap life, or was the "low hanging fruit" of protein catalysis essential from the beginning?**

## Key Research Breakthroughs

### 1. Discovery of Natural Ribozymes (Early 1980s)

**Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman's Nobel-winning work** (early 1980s) demonstrated that RNA could function as an enzyme when they discovered self-splicing introns in *Tetrahymena thermophila* and the catalytic component of RNase P. This proved the basic premise that RNA could have catalytic activity without proteins.

### 2. In Vitro Evolution and Directed Evolution (Late 1980s-Mid 1990s)

The most crucial development came with **in vitro evolution techniques**, independently pioneered by **Jack Szostak** and **Gerald Joyce** in the late 1980s and early 1990s:

**Jack Szostak's lab (early 1990s):**
- Developed systematic methods for evolving RNA molecules with desired catalytic functions
- Used successive cycles of selection, amplification, and mutation to "evolve" ribozymes
- Isolated the first aptamer (RNA molecules that bind specific targets)
- Allowed the discovery of RNA enzymes with completely new functions from random sequence pools

**Directed evolution methodology addressed the amino acid problem by:**
1. **Bypassing natural constraints**: Instead of looking for naturally occurring ribozymes, researchers could evolve them from scratch
2. **Testing catalytic possibilities**: Random RNA libraries of 10^13-10^15 different sequences could be screened for catalytic activity
3. **Demonstrating RNA's catalytic repertoire**: Researchers evolved ribozymes with RNA ligase activity, polymerase activity, and other functions

### 3. Demonstrating Complex Catalytic Capabilities

The research showed that RNA could evolve sophisticated catalytic functions without any protein involvement:

- **RNA ligase ribozymes**: Capable of joining RNA molecules together - essential for replication
- **RNA polymerase ribozymes**: Some developed the ability to extend RNA strands, demonstrating template-directed synthesis
- **Self-sustaining replication systems**: Created systems where RNA molecules could catalyze their own replication in simplified reaction conditions

### 4. Addressing the Protein Efficiency Gap

While ribozymes discovered through these methods were generally slower and less efficient than modern protein enzymes, they were **sufficiently functional** to support key biochemical processes:

**Group I introns** are large self-splicing ribozymes. They catalyze their own excision from mRNA, tRNA and rRNA precursors in a wide range of organisms.[1][2][3] The core secondary structure consists of nine paired regions (P1-P9).[4] These fold to essentially two domains – the P4-P6 domain (formed from the stacking of P5, P4, P6 and P6a helices) and the P3-P9 domain (formed from the P8, P3, P7 and P9 helices).[2] The secondary structure mark-up for this family represents only this conserved core. Group I introns often have long open reading frames inserted in loop regions.

The **hammerhead ribozyme** is an RNA motif that catalyzes reversible cleavage and ligation reactions at a specific site within an RNA molecule. It is one of several catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) known to occur in nature. It serves as a model system for research on the structure and properties of RNA, and is used for targeted RNA cleavage experiments, some with proposed therapeutic applications. Named for the resemblance of early secondary structure diagrams to a hammerhead shark,[1] hammerhead ribozymes were originally discovered in two classes of plant virus-like RNAs: satellite RNAs and viroids. They are also known in some classes of retrotransposons, including the retrozymes.[2] The hammerhead ribozyme motif has been ubiquitously reported in lineages across the tree of life.[3][4]

<document>
<title>Jennifer Doudna</title>
<fragment>
Early in her scientific career, Doudna worked to uncover the structure and biological function of RNA enzymes or ribozymes.[7] While in the Szostak lab, Doudna re-engineered the self-splicing *Tetrahymena* Group I catalytic intron into a true catalytic ribozyme that copied RNA templates.[7] Her focus was on engineering ribozymes and understanding their underlying mechanisms; however, she came to realize that not being able to see the molecular mechanisms of ribozymes was a major problem. Doudna went to the lab of Thomas Cech at the University of Colorado Boulder to crystallize and determine the three-dimensional structure of a ribozyme for the first time, so ribozyme structure could be compared with that of Enzymes, the catalytic Proteins.[7] She started this project at the Cech lab in 1991 and finished it at Yale University in 1996.[14] Doudna joined Yale's Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry as an assistant professor in 1994.[5]

After her PhD, she held research fellowships in molecular biology at the Massachusetts General Hospital and in genetics at Harvard Medical School.[5] From 1991 to 1994, she was Lucille P. Markey Postdoctoral Scholar in Biomedical Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, where she worked with Thomas Cech.[5] As of 2022[update], Doudna has an h-index of 141 according to Google Scholar[9] and of 111 according to Scopus.[29]



### Research on ribozyme structure and function

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Shape of a self-splicing intron with two exons (shown in red and blue). DS Goodsell, 2005, PDB
At Yale, Doudna's group was able to crystallize and solve the three-dimensional structure of the catalytic core of the *Tetrahymena* Group I ribozyme.[7] They showed that a core of five magnesium ions clustered in one region of the P4-P6 domain of the ribozyme, forming a hydrophobic core around which the rest of the structure could fold.[7] This is analogous, but chemically distinct from, the way proteins typically have a core of hydrophobic amino acids.[7] Her group has crystallized other ribozymes,[14] including the Hepatitis Delta Virus ribozyme.[7] This initial work to solve large RNA structures led to further structural studies on an internal ribosome entry site(IRES) and protein-RNA complexes such as the Signal Recognition Particle.[7]

<fragment>
Process in molecular biology

**RNA splicing** is a process in molecular biology where a newly-made precursor messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) transcript is transformed into a mature messenger RNA (mRNA). It works by removing all the introns (non-coding regions of RNA) and *splicing* back together exons (coding regions). For nuclear-encoded genes, splicing occurs in the nucleus either during or immediately after transcription. For those eukaryotic genes that contain introns, splicing is usually needed to create an mRNA molecule that can be translated into protein. For many eukaryotic introns, splicing occurs in a series of reactions which are catalyzed by the spliceosome, a complex of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs). There exist self-splicing introns, that is, ribozymes that can catalyze their own excision from their parent RNA molecule. The process of transcription, splicing and translation is called gene expression, the central dogma of molecular biology.
